program_plain: World: a random network of 400 nodes (mean degree 6). Node types: 2 opinions (random start). Rules each step: a random node picks a random neighbour of a different opinion; with probability 0.95 it cuts that link and links to a random node of its own opinion, otherwise it adopts the neighbour's opinion.
model_family: Opinion dynamics / adaptive (coevolving) voter model on networks (statistical physics, absorbing-state transition)
standard_name: Adaptive / coevolving voter model with rewire-to-same; fragmentation (absorbing) transition
citations: Holme & Newman 2006, Phys Rev E 74, 056108 - original coevolving opinion/network model; dynamics end in disconnected single-opinion components (consensus state); continuous transition
Vazquez, Eguiluz & San Miguel 2008, Phys Rev Lett 100, 108702 - two-state coevolving voter model; absorbing transition at p_c=(mu-2)/(mu-1); active=connected, frozen=fragmented
Kozma & Barrat 2008, Phys Rev E 77, 016102 - consensus formation on adaptive networks; consensus vs fragmented absorbing states
Durrett et al. 2012, PNAS 109, 3682 - graph fission in an evolving voter model; rewire-to-same vs rewire-to-random variants
Opinion dynamics: Statistical physics and beyond, arXiv 2507.11521 (2025) - review; high rewiring gives frozen fragmented phase with two single-opinion components
searches: Holme Newman nonequilibrium phase transition coevolution of networks and opinions
adaptive voter model rewiring fragmentation transition Kozma Barrat consensus time
Vazquez Eguiluz San Miguel generic absorbing transition coevolution dynamics
notes: At p=0.95 and 0.9 (above p_c=0.8 for mean degree 6) theory predicts fast freezing into a fragmented network, typically two components (giant fraction about 0.5, components up). The reported n_giant=1.0 and n_components=-2 look inconsistent with that if they are final-state values; normalisation or sign conventions and measurement time are unknown. The agreement gain (consensus_gain) fits the known behaviour: all edges become concordant at freezing.
full_text:
**Verdict: KNOWN.** The rule system is the adaptive (coevolving) voter model, a statistical-physics model of opinion dynamics. I'm highly confident in the identification, but only moderately confident that the three numeric features match the literature, because two of them look inconsistent with the expected final state (see Caveats).

**1. Model family.** This is opinion dynamics on an adaptive network. The rule is: pick a node and a disagreeing neighbour. With probability p, rewire the link to a random node of the same opinion. Otherwise, copy the neighbour's opinion. This is the Holme–Newman "rewire-to-same" model with two opinions. It is also the Vazquez–Eguíluz–San Miguel coevolving voter model, apart from how the rewired link's new endpoint is chosen.

**2. The behaviour and the earliest sources.**
- **Earliest source:** Holme & Newman (2006) introduced the model. Both update moves reduce the number of neighbouring pairs with different opinions. The network therefore ends up split into disconnected components, each holding a single opinion. They call this the consensus state. The agreement gain is built into the dynamics, and it ends when no disagreeing links remain. The paper reports a continuous phase transition as the balance between rewiring and opinion change varies. It runs from diverse opinions to most individuals sharing one opinion.
- **The same model with two opinions:** Vazquez, Eguíluz & San Miguel (2008) study the same two-state case. A link between opposite-state nodes is rewired with probability p, and otherwise one node takes its neighbour's state. A mean-field analysis gives an absorbing transition from an active to a frozen phase at a critical p_c = (μ-2)/(μ-1), which depends only on the mean degree μ. The active and frozen phases correspond to a connected and a fragmented network respectively.
- **Where your system sits:** with μ = 6, p_c = 0.8. Both p = 0.95 and p = 0.9 are above it, in the frozen, fragmenting regime. They are fast-freezing, high-rewiring variants of the same class.
- **Another source for the same transition:** Kozma & Barrat (2008) describe the long-term states as consensus or a fragmented state. In the fragmented state the network breaks into at least two components, each internally in consensus. The transition is described as a generic absorbing transition.
- **Review:** the recent review "Opinion dynamics: Statistical physics and beyond" (arXiv 2507.11521) summarises it. In finite systems, the active phase below p_c eventually reaches consensus. Above p_c the system freezes into a fragmented phase with two disconnected components, each holding one opinion.

**3. Related work.** Durrett et al., "Graph fission in an evolving voter model", PNAS 2012, analyses the two-opinion rewire-to-same and rewire-to-random variants. The Vazquez et al. citation was checked against the PubMed record (Phys Rev Lett 100(10):108702, 2008) and the arXiv record (0710.4910). The Holme–Newman citation was checked against the APS record (Phys Rev E 74, 056108, 2006).

**Caveats.**
- **Giant component and component count.** The standard result above p_c is a fragmented final network. With two opinions that is typically two components, so the giant fraction is about 0.5 or less, and the component count goes up rather than down. The reported n_giant = 1.0 and n_components = -2.0 don't fit that picture if they are final-state values. I can't tell how these numbers were normalised or signed, or at what time they were measured. If they really are final-state values, the system may not have fragmented at p = 0.95. The cause could be a different rewiring target, a truncated run, or a different measurement. I did not resolve this.
- **Rewiring target.** The literature has both rewire-to-same and rewire-to-random variants. Your rule is rewire-to-same. In the Holme–Newman and Durrett papers, rewire-to-same gives a discontinuous transition.
- **Which node rewires.** The papers differ in details such as which of the two nodes rewires. I do not expect that to change the qualitative behaviour.
